messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Politician
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 42

# Margaret's Story

Margaret sits in the leather chair across from me with her hands folded precisely in her lap, a posture she maintains throughout our sessions. At seventy-seven, she carries herself with the composed dignity that decades in politics have cultivated—shoulders back, chin level, eyes that have learned to hold steady gazes. But there is something else beneath that composure now, something that trembles just underneath the surface.

She was fifty-two when it happened. Her husband, Daniel, was a man she had loved for twenty-eight years by then. They had built a life together—a comfortable life, a respectable life. Margaret was serving her third term in parliament, known for her work on education reform and women's economic empowerment. She had just returned home late from a parliamentary session where she had publicly disagreed with Daniel's business associate on a development project. Daniel was waiting for her in their study.

The argument escalated quickly. He said she had humiliated him, that she had overstepped. When she tried to leave the room, he grabbed her arm. His hand was tight, his voice low and controlled in a way that frightened her more than shouting would have. He pushed her against the wall. She fell, striking her shoulder and head on the corner of a side table. There was blood. There was pain that seemed to split her skull open.

That was twenty-five years ago.

Margaret has never spoken about it publicly. She went to work the next day with careful makeup and a scarf. She told no one—not her closest colleagues, not her sister, not her children. Daniel apologized profusely. He never did it again. They continued their marriage, continued their lives, and Margaret learned to organize her world around the memory of those moments the way one learns to walk around furniture in a familiar room—automatically, without conscious thought.

But the memory has begun to occupy more space as she has aged.

She describes lying awake at night, her heart racing at the memory of his hand on her arm. She cannot quite articulate what triggers these episodes—sometimes it is the sound of a door closing with particular force, sometimes it is nothing she can identify. She simply finds herself back in that study, feeling the impact of the wall against her body, tasting blood. When Daniel reaches for her now, even in affection, her body goes rigid. She has learned to disguise this as arthritis, as the stiffness of age.

At work, Margaret had been a woman known for her quick thinking and decisive action. Now, in the twilight of her political career, she finds herself hesitant in meetings. She second-guesses her positions. When she speaks, she sometimes loses her train of thought, distracted by the sensation of her own heartbeat in her ears. Colleagues have commented that she seems tired, that perhaps it is time to consider retirement.

She retired last year.

Now she spends her days in the home she shares with Daniel, moving through rooms she has inhabited for decades, but which no longer feel entirely safe. She has developed a habit of sitting in the garden in the afternoons, where she can see the gate, where she can monitor the space around her. She reads the newspaper but retains little of what she reads. She attends her granddaughter's school events but struggles to be present in the moment, her attention fractured by hypervigilance.

Margaret tells me these things in measured tones, as though recounting someone else's experience. But her hands, still folded in her lap, have begun to tremble.
